nuggets.title: Viral Super Bowl Ad Pushes Aggregator Partition to 100% CPU

scenario.symptoms: During a marquee sports event, click tracking latencies surge to over 10 seconds. Ingestion gateways report HTTP 503 backpressure errors, while total system throughput drops despite low cluster-wide memory usage.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Monitoring shows that 1 out of 32 Flink subtasks and Kafka partitions is stuck at 100% CPU utilization while the other 31 subtasks are under 10% load. A single viral campaign represents 45% of all incoming clicks.

incident.headline: Hot key partition skew stalls processing pipeline during single-advertiser click spike

agenda.goal: Mitigate single-key CPU bottleneck by introducing key salting and two-stage aggregation.
agenda.opener: One hot ad key is pinning single-partition worker CPU to 100% and stalling ingestion. How do you re-architect stream partitioning to eliminate this hot spot?

evidence.strong: Identifies key skew on ad_id, introduces key salting (e.g., ad_id + random_salt_1..N) to distribute the hot key across multiple stream task instances for stage-1 partial counts, followed by a non-salted stage-2 aggregation step to compute total window counts.
evidence.adequate: Suggests dynamic re-keying or local pre-aggregation, but misses two-stage pipeline architecture or how to recombine salted keys.
evidence.weak: Suggests simply scaling up Kafka partition count or scaling out worker nodes without changing the keying scheme.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes increasing Kafka partitions or Flink cluster size solves hot key CPU saturation.
misconceptions.challenge: All clicks for a single ad_id produce the exact same partition key hash. How does adding more partitions change where that single key lands?

probes: How do you determine the optimal salt range N for high-volume keys without inflating state overhead for long-tail quiet ads?
How do stateful window triggers change when merging partial salted counts in stage two?
hints: Keying directly by ad_id routes all traffic for that ad to a single task slot.
Consider splitting the workload into two phases: partial local counting using an augmented key, then global merging.
agenda.referenceFix: Apply key salting at ingestion by suffixing the partition key with a random integer (ad_id_salt). Stage 1 aggregators summarize counts per salted key per 1-minute window. Stage 2 consumes stage 1 outputs grouped by raw ad_id to produce the unified final count.

nuggets.title: Aggregator Restart Causes Over-Counting in Counter Database

scenario.symptoms: Advertiser dashboards display sudden 2x-3x spikes in aggregate clicks during a 10-minute window, resulting in false budget exhaustion alerts and billing complaints.
scenario.interviewerSetup: A worker node hosting the stream processor crashed and recovered from its latest checkpoint. Upon resumption, offset replay caused previously computed minute counts to be sent to the counter store again.

incident.headline: Replayed stream windows invoke additive INCR mutations on downstream counter store

agenda.goal: Ensure sink updates are idempotent to prevent counter inflation when processing offset replays.
agenda.opener: The stream processor restarted from a checkpoint and replayed uncommitted messages, but counter DB values doubled. Why did checkpointing fail to prevent double counting, and how do you fix it?

evidence.strong: Explains that stream checkpointing guarantees at-least-once processing at the operator level unless downstream storage writes are idempotent or transactional. Replaces additive INCR updates with absolute window overwrite key-value upserts (e.g., SET ad_id:window_start_time = total_count) or two-phase commit sinks.
evidence.adequate: Recognizes that replayed messages invoked non-idempotent operations, suggesting key deduplication or window upserts.
evidence.weak: Claims Kafka exactly-once semantics alone automatically protect external database counter increments.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes stream engine exactly-once config guarantees end-to-end correctness regardless of sink write design.
misconceptions.challenge: If your stream app re-writes count increments to Redis via INCRBY after a crash, what happens to the previously written increment in Redis when the offset is replayed?

probes: What key design allows an external KV store to support deterministic, overwrite-based window updates?
How would you handle out-of-order late click arrivals if you switch from incremental counter additions to full window overwrites?
hints: Incremental updates (INCRBY) are non-idempotent; executing them twice produces wrong state.
Structure sink keys around fixed window bounds so repeated writes replace existing values rather than adding to them.
agenda.referenceFix: Change storage operations from atomic increments to idempotent upserts keyed by exact window boundaries (key: ad_id:window_timestamp). During replay, the worker calculates the total accumulated window count from state and overwrites the exact aggregate value in the database.

nuggets.title: Real-time Metrics Diverge from Advertiser Invoices

scenario.symptoms: Finance reports a persistent 5% discrepancy between daily customer billing statements and live dashboard telemetry, leading to publisher payment disputes.
scenario.interviewerSetup: The real-time streaming aggregator calculates click totals using short-lived duplicate deduplication state (5-minute TTL). Delayed mobile clicks arriving hours later and delayed click-fraud flags are not reflected in real-time counts.

incident.headline: Invoices generated directly from low-latency stream count estimates without batch reconciliation

agenda.goal: Establish a dual-path (Lambda/Kappa) reconciliation mechanism where stream counts drive fast estimates and batch jobs generate official invoices.
agenda.opener: The system relies directly on real-time stream totals to bill clients, missing late clicks and invalid click corrections. How should the architecture be modified for financial correctness?

evidence.strong: Decouples low-latency dashboard counts from financial settlement. Uses raw append-only click logs in object storage to run an offline daily batch reconciliation (e.g. Spark) with full 24-hour deduplication and fraud model scoring as the authoritative billing source of truth.
evidence.adequate: Proposes running a batch job to recalculate numbers, but doesn't explain how dashboard data and billing invoices are isolated or reconciled.
evidence.weak: Suggests increasing streaming TTL deduplication windows indefinitely or running real-time fraud models on streaming instances directly.

misconceptions.pattern: Believes stream aggregation results are complete and accurate enough to directly issue financial invoices.
misconceptions.challenge: What happens when a mobile client syncs 2 hours of offline clicks, or an offline bot detector flags 10,000 invalid clicks overnight? How can a 5-minute stream window handle that?

probes: How do you handle audit trails and telemetry when reconciliation updates previously reported counts?
What SLA thresholds should trigger an engineer alert if batch and streaming counts diverge beyond expected error margins?
hints: Real-time streaming prioritizes speed; batch processing prioritizes completeness and accuracy.
Treat streaming counts as provisional estimates and batch recomputations as immutable source of truth.
agenda.referenceFix: Designate real-time stream outputs as fast, estimated metrics for advertiser operational dashboards. Archive immutable raw click events into object storage. Run a daily batch job to compute precise daily billing tables with full window deduplication and fraud scrubbing, writing final invoice numbers to the billing ledger.
